title: Business disruption: Incumbents must separate experiments credibly
desc: Treats disruption as organized business-model experimentation requiring independent resources and incentives, not automatic AI adoption or inevitable displacement.

kps.k: The cluster frames disruption as business-model change that incumbents must organise for, not as an automatic consequence of adopting AI.
kps.d: Christensen defines disruption through a venture’s movement from low-end or new markets into the mainstream, rather than its technology or initial performance. Tellmann applies this framework to law firms, recommending independent ventures alongside continued improvement of the core business. His argument extends the same innovation scholarship; it does not independently establish that AI is already disrupting legal services along this trajectory.

qs.q: The first minicomputers were disruptive not merely because they were low-end upstarts when they appeared on the scene, nor because they were later heralded as superior to mainframes in many markets; they were disruptive by virtue of the path they followed from the fringe to the mainstream.
qs.a: The Innovator's Dilemma / Disruptive Innovation (Christensen) · Academia · 2015

qs.q: To escape this trap, firms must become structurally ambidextrous; able to invest in  sustaining innovation that advances their core model while simultaneously exploring  disruptive new innovations that may challenge it.
qs.a: Law in the Era of AI: Clients, Firms, and the Future of the Legal Industry · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Established economics and customer expectations can suppress experiments even when firms possess ample expertise and resources.
kps.d: The consulting article argues that processes and priorities responsible for past success constrain new businesses through resource allocation. Tellmann adds that initially weaker performance, lower profitability and rejection by existing customers can prompt leaders to withdraw talent, funding and attention. This diagnosis locates the obstacle in how firms allocate resources and measure success, not simply in technological conservatism.

qs.q: As we teach our Harvard Business School students, the resources, processes, and priorities that an organization acquires and develops for its initial success become sea anchors when it attempts to change course.
qs.a: Consulting on the Cusp of Disruption · Academia · 2013

qs.q: When combined  with negative customer feedback, leaders come to doubt the efficacy or wisdom of  investing in such disruptive technologies, resulting in the withdrawal of the  resources, talent, and leadership attention needed for them to succeed.
qs.a: Law in the Era of AI: Clients, Firms, and the Future of the Legal Industry · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Consulting supplies a precedent for weakening professional-service protections, but not proof of inevitable legal-market displacement.
kps.d: Christensen, Wang and van Bever’s 2013 article argues that accessible data, experienced buyers, alternative staffing and automation enable clients to internalise or divide work previously bought from one-stop consultancies. It reports declining classic-strategy work and cites BeyondCore and Motista as examples of analytical automation and lower-cost delivery. These observations and company claims are not industry-wide employment measurements. Interviewed consultants counter that enduring client needs, reputation and limits to commoditisation protect incumbents; the authors reject those reassurances while acknowledging uncertainty about disruption’s timing.

qs.q: The vast turnover at consultancies means armies of experienced strategists are available for hire by former clients, whose increasing sophistication allows them to allocate work instead of relying on one-stop shops as they did in the past.
qs.a: Consulting on the Cusp of Disruption · Academia · 2013

qs.q: The big data company BeyondCore can automatically evaluate vast amounts of data, identify statistically relevant insights, and present them through an animated briefing, rendering the junior analyst role obsolete.
qs.a: Consulting on the Cusp of Disruption · Academia · 2013

kps.k: Operational separation must include independent funding, commercial decisions and incentives—not merely a separate organisational label.
kps.d: The consulting article recommends a fully capable autonomous unit, experienced leaders, protected funding, independent sales channels, a different profit formula and sustained CEO protection. Tellmann adapts this prescription to law firms: let ventures set their own pricing and strategy, assess growth, learning and capabilities rather than profits per partner, and reward experimentation and customer feedback rather than billable hours. These are organisational prescriptions; the supplied material does not quantify their effectiveness.

qs.q: **An autonomous business unit.** The unit should have all the functional skills it needs to succeed, freeing it from reliance on the parent organization, and it must not report to the business or businesses that are being disrupted.
qs.a: Consulting on the Cusp of Disruption · Academia · 2013

qs.q: It  should be given full authority to invest in new models and chart its own strategy  independent of the KPIs, cost-structures, and culture of the legacy parent.
qs.a: Law in the Era of AI: Clients, Firms, and the Future of the Legal Industry · Academia · 2026

kps.k: The proposed strategy starts with overlooked customers and small experiments, while preserving learning links to the parent.
kps.d: Tellmann recommends targeting customers outside the legacy firm’s focus who find established services too expensive or unsuitable. Ventures can test pricing, delivery and technology without incumbent expectations, then scale validated ideas progressively. A portfolio spreads experimentation across multiple bets and preserves resources after failures. Autonomy should not mean isolation: ventures should return lessons to the parent, although adoption by the core remains a possibility rather than a promised outcome.

qs.q: The start-up’s focus  should therefore be on seeking out and addressing the needs of customer and  market segments that currently sit outside of the legacy firm’s focus.
qs.a: Law in the Era of AI: Clients, Firms, and the Future of the Legal Industry · Academia · 2026

qs.q: Instead, iterative learning and incremental improvements within the start-up can  should be allowed to unfold, with promising proofs of concept scaled progressively  as they are validated.
qs.a: Law in the Era of AI: Clients, Firms, and the Future of the Legal Industry · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Self-disruption requires tolerance of eventual internal competition, not immediate abandonment of profitable work.
kps.d: Christensen advises sustaining the core and addressing customer cannibalisation when it becomes real; substitution may take decades or remain incomplete. The consulting article places greater emphasis on accepting competition now, asking whether McKinsey Solutions can sell without a full engagement team. Tellmann’s ClearyX example expresses an ambition to build a business capable of displacing its parent, while his small-scale approach seeks to avoid premature internal resistance. These are differences of emphasis and sequencing, not a demonstrated disagreement over outcomes: neither venture example supplies measured commercial success.

qs.q: Incumbent companies do need to respond to disruption if it’s occurring, but they should not overreact by dismantling a still-profitable business.
qs.a: The Innovator's Dilemma / Disruptive Innovation (Christensen) · Academia · 2015

qs.q: Will the partnership blink when a nontraditional client requests delivery of McKinsey Solutions without obligatory use of a full engagement team?
qs.a: Consulting on the Cusp of Disruption · Academia · 2013

kps.k: Competitive entry and better technology do not, by themselves, establish disruption.
kps.d: Christensen distinguishes peripheral competition, a disruptive market trajectory and direct attacks on core customers; the latter may provoke stronger incumbent innovation. Consistently, the consulting article leaves open whether the Big Four’s expansion into consulting will create new business models or copy established ones. The practical implication is to diagnose the entrant’s customers, economics and development path before selecting a response, rather than treating every technology-led competitor as an existential threat.

qs.q: For example, small competitors that nibble away at the periphery of your business very likely should be ignored—unless they are on a disruptive trajectory, in which case they are a potentially mortal threat.
qs.a: The Innovator's Dilemma / Disruptive Innovation (Christensen) · Academia · 2015

qs.q: Whether they’ll attempt to create a disruptive business model or just copy the incumbents’ business model remains to be seen.
qs.a: Consulting on the Cusp of Disruption · Academia · 2013

vlens.an: The selected academia and research sources directly support the proposition that disruption is a business-model trajectory requiring credible organisational separation, rather than an automatic consequence of adopting AI or other technology. Their common reasoning is that incumbent resource-allocation processes, customer expectations, performance metrics and profit formulas systematically disadvantage experiments that initially serve peripheral markets or perform differently from the core. They therefore recommend autonomous operations with protected funding, distinct leadership, commercial authority and incentives, while continuing to sustain the profitable incumbent business. Material variation lies mainly in scope and sequencing: Christensen supplies the general conceptual distinction between technology and disruption and advises against premature abandonment of the core; Christensen, Wang and van Bever apply the theory to consulting and more strongly emphasise tolerating competition between new and existing offerings; Tellmann adapts these prescriptions to law firms through small experiments, portfolios of ventures and learning links back to the parent. The evidential bases also differ: the general theory invokes prior research, the consulting article combines observations and examples with predictions, and Tellmann provides organisational reasoning and the ClearyX illustration without measured evidence of commercial success. These curated sources therefore align on the strategic prescription while leaving the timing, effectiveness and legal-market consequences unproven.

qs.q: Disrupters tend to focus on getting the business model, rather than merely the product, just right.
qs.a: The Innovator's Dilemma / Disruptive Innovation (Christensen) · Academia · 2015

qs.q: Create an independent start up  A better way to go, according to Christensen and subsequent scholars is to  acknowledge these dynamics and set up a separate organisational structure for the  disruptive venture; one that is modelled on a start-up, operationally independent from  the legacy ﬁrm and dedicated to disruptive innovation.753  The start-up should have its own leadership, organisation, budget, and mandate.
qs.a: Law in the Era of AI: Clients, Firms, and the Future of the Legal Industry · Academia · 2026

elens.an: The pre-2015 source supports the proposition that disruption in professional services is fundamentally an organisational and business-model challenge rather than an automatic result of adopting technology. It argues that incumbents’ established resources, processes, priorities and resource-allocation logic can suppress new models, even where the firm has strong expertise and substantial resources. Its concrete prescription closely matches the cluster’s emphasis on credible separation: an autonomous, fully capable unit, protected funding, independent sales channels, distinct profit logic and sustained CEO protection. It also supports the need to tolerate competition with the core business, illustrated by the unresolved question of whether McKinsey would permit clients to buy McKinsey Solutions without a traditional engagement team. Material nuance lies in the article’s stronger prediction that consulting disruption is inevitable, while conceding uncertainty about its timing and trajectory; its examples of automation and alternative delivery are illustrative company observations rather than industry-wide proof of displacement. It also distinguishes competitive entry from disruption, leaving open whether the Big Four would create a new business model or merely imitate incumbents. Because this time-period facet contains one curated source, the conclusion describes that source’s relationship to the proposition and does not establish broader prevalence among pre-2015 commentators.

qs.q: As we teach our Harvard Business School students, the resources, processes, and priorities that an organization acquires and develops for its initial success become sea anchors when it attempts to change course.
qs.a: Consulting on the Cusp of Disruption · Academia · 2013

qs.q: **A separate resource allocation process.** This will fund the unit regardless of the fortunes of the core business.
qs.a: Consulting on the Cusp of Disruption · Academia · 2013

elens.an: The period’s supplied source supports the proposition that disruption is an evolving business-model and market trajectory, not an automatic consequence of adopting a particular technology. It also supports the incumbent strategy at the proposition’s core: maintain and improve the profitable established business while placing disruptive opportunities in a separate operation. Internal variation concerns sequencing and limits rather than the core position. The source cautions that substitution may be slow or incomplete, that not every entrant or technological improvement is disruptive, and that incumbents should avoid prematurely dismantling the core or resolving possible cannibalisation before it occurs. It recommends organisational separation, but the supplied material does not establish the more detailed requirements in the cluster synthesis—such as independent incentives, sales channels and performance measures—or quantify separation’s effectiveness. Because this time-period evidence contains one curated source, it shows that source’s alignment rather than broader prevalence.

qs.a: The Innovator's Dilemma / Disruptive Innovation (Christensen) · Academia · 2015

qs.q: Our research suggests that the success of this new enterprise depends in large part on keeping it separate from the core business.
qs.a: The Innovator's Dilemma / Disruptive Innovation (Christensen) · Academia · 2015

elens.an: The 2026 source directly supports the proposition that disruption is not an automatic result of AI adoption but an organisational challenge requiring credible separation of business-model experiments from the incumbent firm. Tellmann attributes resistance to legacy economics, customer expectations, performance measures and resource-allocation processes, then prescribes an operationally independent start-up with its own leadership, budget, mandate and authority to depart from the parent’s KPIs, cost structures and culture. He also supports continued improvement of the core business, small and progressively scaled experiments, distinct pricing and incentives, and feedback of lessons to the parent. Internal variation concerns implementation and sequencing rather than the proposition itself: autonomy must coexist with knowledge transfer; experiments should aspire to possible self-disruption while initially remaining small enough to limit internal resistance; and ClearyX illustrates the intended structure and ambition but does not provide measured evidence that this model succeeds commercially. Because this time period contains one curated source, no broader prevalence or cross-source consensus can be inferred.
